units.t: Stoicism. Episode two.
In this episode: Seneca: time, anger and wealth, Marcus Aurelius: the philosopher emperor and Stoic practices for modern life.
Part one. Seneca: time, anger and wealth.
Playwright, statesman, millionaire, adviser to Nero.
Seneca wrote brilliantly about living well, and struggled to live up to it.
A flawed Stoic.
Lucius Annaeus Seneca, about 4 BC to AD 65, was born in Córdoba, Spain, and became a leading Roman writer, orator and senator.
In AD 41 Emperor Claudius exiled him to Corsica, accused of adultery with the emperor's niece, and he spent eight years there.
Recalled in 49, he became tutor and then chief adviser to the young Nero.
For several years he helped steer the empire, and he grew enormously rich.
Critics, then and now, call him a hypocrite: a Stoic preaching simplicity while living in luxury and serving a tyrant.
Seneca himself admitted he fell far short of his ideals.
Time and letters.
In On the Shortness of Life, Seneca argued: 'It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it.'
People guard their money carefully but give their time to anyone who asks.
They postpone living until retirement, as if they were guaranteed to reach it.
His remedy: treat time as your most precious possession, spend it deliberately and live fully today.
Late in life, Seneca wrote 124 surviving letters to his friend Lucilius, a Roman official in Sicily.
Each tackles a practical theme: friendship, grief, fear, old age, wealth, even noisy neighbours.
They are personal and warm, often starting with something from his day.
They read like advice from a wise, flawed friend.
On anger.
In On Anger, Seneca called anger a brief insanity that harms the angry person more than its target.
His strategies sound strikingly modern.
Delay your response, since time cools anger.
Notice the early warning signs.
Avoid provoking people and situations when you're tired or hungry.
Imagine how you look when furious.
And consider that the other person may not have meant harm, or that you've done the same yourself.
He praised Plato, who, furious with a slave, asked his nephew Speusippus to deal with the man instead, because he was angry, and so in no state to judge.
Poverty and grief.
In one letter, Seneca advised setting aside a few days now and then to live on the cheapest food and roughest clothing, then asking, 'Is this what I feared?'
The point was freedom, not self-punishment.
Once you know you can cope with little, the fear of losing things loosens, and you can enjoy what you have without clinging to it.
Modern versions include a week of simple meals or a spending freeze.
Seneca also wrote consolations, comforting the bereaved.
One went to Marcia, still mourning her son three years on.
Another went to his mother, Helvia, from exile.
He did not urge suppressing grief: our eyes should be neither dry nor overflowing.
We may weep, but not wail.
Be grateful for the time you had, and gradually return to life.
Plays and a Stoic death.
Seneca also wrote tragedies, including Medea, Phaedra, Oedipus and Thyestes, full of revenge and overwhelming passion, perhaps showing what happens when emotions go unchecked.
They influenced Elizabethan dramatists such as Thomas Kyd and William Shakespeare.
His Natural Questions investigated earthquakes, comets and thunder.
For Seneca, studying nature lifted the mind above petty worries.
In AD 65 Nero accused Seneca of involvement in the Pisonian conspiracy and ordered him to take his own life.
According to the historian Tacitus, he faced it calmly, told weeping friends to remember the philosophy they had studied and left them 'the image of his life'.
His composure became a famous model of Stoic courage.
The key idea: Seneca was a Roman philosopher and adviser to Nero who admitted falling short of his own ideals.
Part two. Marcus Aurelius: the philosopher emperor.
The most powerful man in the world wrote private notes to himself about staying humble, patient and good.
They became one of history's most-read books.
The philosopher emperor.
Marcus was born in AD 121 into a wealthy Roman family.
Emperor Hadrian noticed him and arranged for his chosen successor, Antoninus Pius, to adopt Marcus and prepare him for power.
Marcus studied intensely and loved philosophy.
His Stoic tutor Junius Rusticus lent him his own copy of the teachings of Epictetus, a gift Marcus recorded with gratitude.
He became emperor in 161 and insisted on sharing power with his adoptive brother, Lucius Verus, until Verus died in 169.
Historians count Marcus as the last of the 'Five Good Emperors', a period of relative stability.
He is the only Roman emperor remembered mainly as a philosopher.
A troubled reign.
Despite his wish for a quiet life, Marcus spent much of his reign at war.
Rome fought the Parthian Empire in the east, then he spent years on the Danube frontier fighting Germanic peoples such as the Marcomanni.
The Antonine Plague, probably smallpox, was brought back by returning troops and spread through the empire, killing millions by many estimates.
In 175 a trusted general, Avidius Cassius, rebelled after a false rumour of Marcus's death.
Several of Marcus's children died young.
His writings show a man constantly trying to stay calm and decent amid pressure, loss and exhaustion.
Notes to himself.
Marcus wrote notes to himself in Greek, many during military campaigns.
One section is headed 'Among the Quadi', a tribe he fought.
We call the collection the Meditations, but the title in the manuscripts means something like 'To Himself'.
These are not a polished book.
They are reminders, repeated in different words, of principles he struggled to live by.
That is part of their power: we're reading an emperor's honest efforts to be better.
Book 2 opens by telling yourself at the start of the day that you'll meet meddling, ungrateful, arrogant people.
They act this way because they don't know good from bad.
We are made for cooperation, like hands or the two rows of teeth, so you can't be harmed by them or angry with them.
Key themes.
Marcus returns again and again to a few ideas.
Everything is temporary: even emperors and empires are soon forgotten, so don't chase fame.
Focus on the present task, doing it as if it were the last act of your life.
Accept what happens as part of nature's order.
Do your duty to others, since we are made to work together.
And look at things as they are, stripped of grand labels: fine wine is fermented grape juice, and a purple imperial robe is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish.
Seeing plainly takes the heat out of craving and envy.
Death and legacy.
Marcus died in AD 180 on the Danube frontier, probably of illness.
Unlike the four emperors before him, he had a surviving son, and he made Commodus his heir.
Commodus proved erratic and cruel, fought as a gladiator and was assassinated in 192.
Historians often mark Marcus's death as the end of Rome's golden age.
Only a few manuscripts of the Meditations survived the Middle Ages.
The first printed edition appeared in 1559, and the book has been in print ever since.
Readers have included Frederick the Great, the poet Matthew Arnold and Bill Clinton, along with countless ordinary people.
Its appeal is simple: if the man who ruled the Roman Empire struggled with anger, grief and self-doubt, and kept trying anyway, so can the rest of us.
The key idea: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from AD 161 to 180 and is remembered chiefly as a philosopher.
Part three. Stoic practices for modern life.
Stoicism was always meant to be practised, not just studied.
Eight exercises you can start today, most taking less than five minutes.
Rehearse your day.
Like Marcus Aurelius, spend a few minutes each morning previewing the day.
What might go wrong?
A late train, a tense meeting, a child who won't get ready for school?
How do you want to act if it does?
This isn't pessimism.
It's rehearsal, the same reason athletes visualise a race and pilots practise emergencies in simulators.
Two or three situations is plenty.
Add what modern Stoics call the reserve clause.
Seneca's wise person says, 'I will sail, unless something prevents me.'
Commit fully to the goal, but silently add 'fate permitting'.
If a storm cancels the flight, you haven't failed at what was in your control.
Widen your view.
The Stoics practised premeditatio malorum: briefly imagining the loss of your health, a loved one or your home.
It sounds grim, but it often brings a rush of appreciation, pushing back against hedonic adaptation, our habit of getting used to good things.
Keep it brief and gentle.
If it triggers real anxiety, drop it and focus on gratitude instead.
Marcus Aurelius also pictured life from above: cities, armies, weddings and funerals, all small against vast time.
Try seeing your problem from a plane, then from orbit.

Research led by Ethan Kross suggests that self-distancing, even talking to yourself as 'you' or by name instead of 'I', can reduce emotional reactivity and help people reason more wisely about conflicts.
Guard your conduct.
In his 11th letter to Lucilius, Seneca passed on a tip he borrowed from Epicurus: choose a person of fine character and live as though they were always watching.
He suggested Cato, or the gentler Laelius if Cato seemed too stern.
The point isn't fear of judgement.
It's that a respected witness helps you act on your better instincts.
When you're about to snap or cut a corner, ask what they'd do.
Talk less, too.
Zeno said we have two ears and one mouth so we can listen more than we speak.
Epictetus urged saying only what's needed, and avoiding gossip.
Before speaking, ask whether it needs saying.
Disarm insults.
Epictetus advised that if you're told someone has been speaking badly of you, don't defend yourself.
Say, 'He obviously didn't know my other faults, or he'd have mentioned those too.'
Seneca tells how Cato was struck in a public bathhouse by a man who didn't recognise him.
When the man later apologised, Cato replied, 'I don't remember being hit.'
The idea is that an insult only harms you if you accept it as harm.
Next time you're criticised, ask whether any of it is true.
If it is, learn from it.
If it isn't, it says more about them.
Humour often ends the fight.
The evening review.
Seneca reviewed each day before sleep, asking: What bad habit did I cure today?
What fault did I resist?
In what way am I better?
He did it without harshness, like a kind teacher, forgiving himself while noting what to change.
Try writing three lines each night: one thing you did well, one thing you'd do differently, and one thing you're grateful for.
It takes about five minutes.
Over weeks, patterns appear, such as which situations reliably set you off.
That self-awareness is the foundation of every other Stoic practice.
The key idea: Preview the day's likely difficulties each morning, decide how you will respond, and hold your plans lightly.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do critics call Seneca a hypocrite?
Answer. He preached simplicity yet lived in luxury.
Question two. What made Marcus Aurelius unusual among Roman emperors?
Answer. He is remembered chiefly as a philosopher.
Question three. Why preview the day's likely problems each morning?
Answer. It lets you choose your response in advance.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
